name: Teda
confidence_why: Nothing first-hand describes where stress falls in Teda: Lukas (1953) says only that Tubu, chiefly the Dazaga dialects, has a strong stress accent whose distribution still needed study, Tucker and Bryan (1966) repeat this and add from Le Coeur (1956) that Teda lacks an elaborate tone system, and Dybo (1987, 1995), re-analysing Lukas's accent marks, derives a free accent on the first high-toned syllable with just three Teda forms in a footnote, so any placement or type for Teda proper would be a guess.

sweep_summary: Tedaga is not in the catalog. The only title-search hit, Dybo 1994 (English, St. Petersburg Journal of African Studies 2: 29-50; 3: 27-44), has no open copy anywhere I could reach (inslav.ru posts only the Russian versions; archive.org, Crossref, Glottolog give no copy; Its Russian text, Dybo 1995 (MLJ 1: 236-279), was already held by the project from the daza1242 check; I re-read the relevant pages by eye (pp. 238, 240, 263, 269), rendered fresh page scan, and saved verbatim quotes with English translations at, logged in there. Dybo's finding: Tubu (Lukas 1953's data, chiefly Dazaga with Tedaga as 'northern dialect') has a paradigmatic, non-fixed accent governed by a Balto-Slavic-type contour rule -- stress on the first high-toned (dominant) syllable of the word-form; verbs divide into barytone (root-stressed, high-toned root) and oxytone (final-stressed, low-toned root) classes; Lukas gave no placement rule and the noun data are too thin. Tedaga-specific evidence is limited to three verb forms in fn. 18, p. 263, showing the same split. This is a Tebu-group statement from a secondary reanalysis, so for a Tedaga-proper coding the first-hand sources remain Lukas 1953 (De Gruyter, paywalled DOI 10.1515/9783112766194) and Le Coeur & Le Coeur 1956 (print only), both already flagged in this directory's earlier record. Acquisition priority for the 1994 English printing: medium (same content as the Russian text already read; useful only for quoting in English).

new_statements.translation: The Tubu language possesses a strong (dynamic) accent, which gives the language an energetic character. In what way the accent is distributed rhythmically within the sentence requires closer investigation. Tone also plays a role in Tubu that should not be underestimated. [...] Despite these limitations it would be wrong to belittle the importance of tone in Tubu. It does exist, though to a lesser extent, as word-distinguishing tone or as form-distinguishing tone [...] — Placing the stress in the word-form, by contrast, caused Lukas no difficulty, so he accents every example in the book without, however, giving any general rule that would determine the place of stress in the word-form.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tubu (Lukas's description) is a tone language with a strong dynamic stress accent on top; Lukas marks the stressed high tone in every word but states no rule for where it falls, and says its rhythmic placement in the sentence is unstudied. Dybo's reading of Lukas's accented data (p. 240) is that stress is not fixed relative to word edges and that verbs split into a root-stressed (barytone) and an end-stressed (oxytone) accent type, i.e. lexically/morphologically assigned accent. No fixed-position rule exists in any source seen.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; Dybo (p. 240 fn. 2) notes Lukas does not describe accent behaviour in noun phrases and the material is too small to conclude anything.
new_statements.domain_note: Lukas's statement concerns the sentence (rhythmic distribution) and word-level tone; Dybo's accent types concern the verbal word-form. The description is of 'Tubu' as recorded by Lukas, i.e. chiefly the Keshirda dialect of Dazaga (daza1242) with Tedaga only as 'northern dialect' notes; nothing Tedaga-specific was accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: The only accent statement found is Lukas 1953:7 on 'Tubu', reached second-hand through Dybo 1995/1987 (held in the daza1242 folder). Lukas's Tubu is, per Walters 2015 (pp. 13-14) and Dybo's own dialect labels, chiefly the Keshirda dialect of Dazaga (daza1242), with Tedaga (teda1241) appearing only as 'Norddialekt' notes; WALS files Lukas 1953 and Le Coeur 1956 under Tubu = tebu1238 (the Tebu group). So the statement is a group-level (tebu1238) statement resting on Dazaga data, not a Tedaga-specific one. The Tedaga-specific description (Le Coeur & Le Coeur 1956, Tibesti Teda) was not accessible. The open Bardaï (Tibesti) orthography materials are Tedaga proper but say nothing about stress.

new_statements.quote: Внутренняя реконструкция (анализ системы в терминах акцентуационных валентностей и сравнение результатов с тоновыми схемами III глагольной группы), подтверждаемая непосредственным сравнением с тонами канури, позволяет установить, что акцент в тубу регулируется контурным правилом балто-славянского типа, т.е. акцент падает на начало первой последовательности морфем (соответственно, слогов) высшей валентности, иначе говоря, на первый слог с высоким тоном (соответственно, с восходящим или нисходящим тоном, которые приравниваются в контурном правиле к высокому).
new_statements.translation: Internal reconstruction (analysis of the system in terms of accentual valencies and comparison of the results with the tone schemes of verb group III), confirmed by direct comparison with the tones of Kanuri, allows us to establish that accent in Tubu is governed by a contour rule of the Balto-Slavic type, i.e. the accent falls on the beginning of the first sequence of morphemes (respectively syllables) of the higher valency -- in other words, on the first high-toned syllable (or the first syllable with a rising or falling tone, which the contour rule treats as high).
new_statements.citation: Dybo, V. A. 1995. Akcentuacionnye processy v jazykakh gruppy teda-kanuri i problema proiskhozhdenija paradigmaticheskikh akcentnykh sistem. Moskovskij lingvisticheskij zhurnal 1: 236-279 (Russian text of Dybo 1994, St. Petersburg Journal of African Studies 2: 29-50; 3: 27-44). Based on Lukas 1953, Die Sprache der Tubu in der zentralen Sahara.
new_statements.locator: p. 269 (p. 18 right); supporting pp. 240 and 263 fn. 18
new_statements.reading: Word stress in Tubu is not fixed to a word edge: it is a paradigmatic (lexically/morphologically conditioned) accent whose position is predictable from tone -- the first high-toned (dominant) syllable of the word-form. Verbs split into barytone (root-stressed, high-toned root) and oxytone (final-stressed, low-toned root) classes (p. 240); no rule is statable for nouns (p. 240 fn. 2). Caveat on identity: Dybo's 'Tubu' is Lukas 1953's material, chiefly Dazaga (Keshirda); Tedaga enters only as the 'northern dialect' in fn. 18, p. 263 (hanā.nər.ín 'I don't know' vs barytone ráŋər.in 'I can't'; ké.dak.e.n 'he doesn't want'), which shows the same two-class pattern. It is a second-hand analysis of Lukas's accent marks, not fresh fieldwork on Tedaga.

In TUBU, tone is important, but tonal patterns apparently fluctuate and are difficult to follow. Tone can, however, have both lexical and grammatical significance. [...] Lukas records High and Low tone, also Rising tone [...] Only High tone is consistently marked in his examples. [...] Nothing is known about Stress in KANURI; Lukas mentions (but does not illustrate) a strong 'Akzent (Druck)' in TUBU, which may apparently affect tones. new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule. The chapter reports, at second hand, that Le Cœur finds Teda without an elaborate tonal system and leaves tone unmarked; that in Tubu (Lukas's southern material) tone is important but fluctuating and has lexical and grammatical uses; that nothing is known of stress in Kanuri; and that Lukas reports, without examples, a strong stress accent in Tubu that may affect tones. Vowel length in Teda-Tubu is 'perhaps associated with stress'. Where the stress falls is not stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's chapter (p. 168) defines TEDA (TUDA) as the northern dialects with examples from Le Cœur (italicized) and TUBU as the southern dialects (DAZA, KASHIRDA 'dialect from which most of Lukas's examples are taken', KREDA), plus KANURI (Lukas) and ZAGHAWA (Stevenson). The tone remark for TEDA is Le Cœur's; the tone doublets, the High/Low/Rising tones and the strong 'Akzent (Druck)' are Lukas's TUBU (Kashirda/Daza) data, not Teda proper. The 'length is perhaps associated with stress' sentence is said of TEDA-TUBU jointly.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the catalog's own source (world-r3 record cites Tucker & Bryan 1966 p. 170 sec. 2); the held fragments reproduce the catalog quote and the existing verified statement word for word. Adds nothing on placement; consistent in type with the Lukas-via-Dybo statement (tone plus a strong stress accent, said of Tubu rather than Teda proper). No alternative open copy exists to upgrade the snippet-level read to a full-page read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule. For TEDA proper (Le Coeur's northern material) the chapter reports no elaborate tonal system and no tone marking; for TUBU (Lukas's southern/Kashirda material) tone is lexically and grammatically significant but fluctuating, and Lukas reports a strong stress accent ('Akzent (Druck)') that may affect tones; vowel length in Teda-Tubu is 'perhaps associated with stress'. Second-hand from Le Coeur 1956 and Lukas 1953:7.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's 'TEDA (TUDA)' = northern dialects, examples from Le Coeur 1956 (Tedaga proper, teda1241); their 'TUBU' = southern dialects (Daza, Kashirda from Lukas 1953, Kreda), i.e. chiefly Dazaga (daza1242). The tone facts and the 'Akzent (Druck)' remark are said of TUBU (Lukas's Kashirda material); of TEDA proper the chapter says only that Le Coeur reports no elaborate tonal system and does not mark tone, and (for Teda-Tubu jointly) that length is perhaps associated with stress.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress placement, because no source states one for Teda. Mild tension on tone: Tucker & Bryan 1966:170 relay Le Cœur's view that Teda (northern dialects) 'differs from KANURI in not having an elaborate tonal system' and that he does not mark tone, whereas Dybo 1995 builds a tone-derived accent analysis on Lukas's Tubu (Kashirda) accent marks and treats Teda as the northern dialect of the same system (fn. 18, p. 263). The stress statement itself is the same in both: Lukas's strong 'Akzent (Druck)', which Tucker & Bryan note Lukas 'mentions (but does not illustrate)' — so the only first-hand stress claim for the group remains Lukas 1953:7, unlocated as to placement.
